  SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-16349                                        BEFORE THE STATE
  PUC DOCKET NO. 59475                                                     OFFICE
                                                                             OF
  JOINT APPLICATION OF ONCOR                                           ADMINISTRATIVE
  ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY LLC                                          HEARINGS
  AND LCRA TRANSMISSION SERVICES
  CORPORATION TO AMEND THEIR
  CERTIFICATES OF CONVENIENCE
  AND NECESSITY FOR THE BELL
  COUNTY EAST SWITCH TO BIG HILL
  SUBSTATION 765-KV TRANSMISSION
  LINE PROJECT


       INTERVENOR STACY RANDOLPH'S PROPOSED FINDINGS OF FACT,
            CONCLUSIONS OF LAW, AND ORDERING PARAGRAPHS
                                       Filed June 26, 2026

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:
        Intervenor Stacy Randolph, appearing pro se, respectfully files these Proposed Findings
of Fact, Conclusions of Law, and Ordering Paragraphs based on her Reply to Initial Post-Hearing
Briefs, her Initial Post-Hearing Brief, the cross-examination record, and the record evidence
cited in those filings. Ms. Randolph appears as the daughter of Aaron Edward Howton and Nelda
Howton and as an heir to the Howton properties. She requests that the Administrative Law
Judges recommend rejection of Applicants' Route 894 and any route using Link F20, and
recommend Route 296 or, in the alternative, Route 899, Route 499, Route 767, Route 295, or
another route that avoids Link F20.

                             I. PROPOSED FINDINGS OF FACT
1.   Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation
     filed a joint application to amend their certificates of convenience and necessity for the Bell
     County East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765-kV Transmission Line Project.
2.   The proposed project is a high-voltage 765-kV transmission line project that would cross
     multiple counties and affect rural landowners, family homesteads, agricultural properties,
     community resources, environmental resources, and cultural-resource areas.
3.   Stacy Randolph is a pro se intervenor in this docket.
4.   Ms. Randolph is the daughter of Aaron Edward Howton and Nelda Howton and is an heir
     to the Howton properties.



                                              Page 1
 5.   Ms. Randolph's position is based on her family knowledge, personal observations, and
     future interest in the Howton family property.
6.   The Howton property is a family residence and working rural property used for livestock,
     poultry, gardening, hunting, outdoor family activities, and ordinary agricultural operations.
     Stacy Randolph Initial Post-Hearing Brief, PUC Interchange Item No. 6210.
7.   Link F20 would impose a permanent industrial burden on Ms. Randolph's parents'
     residence, agricultural land, family inheritance interests, and the Cedar Valley community.
8.   The 765-kV transmission line would be a long-term encumbrance on property that Ms.
     Randolph and future family members expect to inherit, use, maintain, and protect.
9.   Ms. Randolph opposes certification of Applicants' Route 894 and opposes any route using
     Link F20.
10. Ms. Randolph supports Route 296 as the preferred non-F20 route and, alternatively,
    supports Route 899, Route 499, Route 767, Route 295, or another route that avoids Link
    F20.
11. Applicants and Route 894-supporting parties rely heavily on route-wide tables, generalized
    cost figures, reported habitable-structure counts, and assurances that later mitigation will
    address site-specific concerns.
12. Those route-wide tables and later-mitigation assurances do not resolve the link-level
    problems shown in the record for Link F20.
13. The record shows that Applicants' environmental information and routing counts for Link
    F20 were developed primarily from desktop review, aerial review, GIS mapping, and other
    non-ground-level sources.
14. Applicants' witness did not personally walk Link F20 and did not obtain the kind of local
    field information necessary to identify site-specific constraints before relying on F20 in
    Route 894. Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 120:18-124:8, PUC Interchange Item No. 6137.
15. Applicants did not adequately verify the F20 habitable-structure count by boots-on-the-
    ground observation before relying on F20 in the comparative route analysis.
16. The Carl Simpson residence was identified during cross-examination as approximately 383
    feet from Link F20, within the 500-foot habitable-structure distance. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at
    51:8-52:21, PUC Interchange Item No. 6137.
17. Applicants' witness acknowledged that, based on the graphic shown during cross-
    examination, the Carl Simpson residence appeared to be within the relevant distance.
    Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 51:8-52:21, PUC Interchange Item No. 6137.
18. Applicants' witness further acknowledged that, if the structure meets Applicants' habitable-
    structure standard, Applicants would adjust the F20 count. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 52:15-21,
    PUC Interchange Item No. 6137.


                                              Page 2
 19. Cross-examination and local evidence therefore revealed discrepancies and omissions in the
    F20 data, including the habitable-structure count.
20. Applicants did not conduct a site-specific Golden-cheeked Warbler habitat field survey on
    Link F20 before route selection. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 52:23-54:8, PUC Interchange Item
    No. 6137.
21. Applicants' F20 endangered-species figure was based on GIS or U.S. Fish and Wildlife
    Service mapping rather than field verification. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 52:23-54:8, PUC
    Interchange Item No. 6137.
22. The record raises unresolved Golden-cheeked Warbler habitat and U.S. Fish and Wildlife
    Service concerns near Link F20.
23. First Cedar Valley Baptist Church is a longstanding community, cultural, historical, and
    aesthetic resource near Link F20.
24. The record identifies First Cedar Valley Baptist Church as established in or about 1942 and
    located approximately 690 to 720 feet from the F20 centerline. Aaron Edward Howton
    Initial Post-Hearing Brief, PUC Interchange Item No. 6257; First Cedar Valley Baptist
    Church filing, PUC Interchange Item No. 5925.
25. Ms. Randolph's Initial Post-Hearing Brief emphasized First Cedar Valley Baptist Church's
    role as a community and disaster gathering place. Stacy Randolph Initial Post-Hearing
    Brief, PUC Interchange Item No. 6210.
26. Applicants did not adequately reflect First Cedar Valley Baptist Church in the F20 cultural-
    resource analysis.
27. A routing analysis that shows no relevant cultural resources for F20 is materially
    incomplete when a longstanding church and community landmark lies within the review
    area.
28. Buttermilk Creek and the surrounding area raise historical, archaeological, and cultural-
    resource concerns relevant to route selection.
29. The record indicates that Applicants did not field-survey the archaeologically sensitive
    Buttermilk Creek drainage before selecting F20 and that F20 crosses high archaeological-
    potential areas. Aaron Edward Howton Initial Post-Hearing Brief, PUC Interchange Item
    No. 6257.
30. Applicants' Environmental Assessment did not reference the April 12, 2022 EF-3 tornado
    through Cedar Valley. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 54:10-14, PUC Interchange Item No. 6137.
31. Applicants' witness confirmed that the routing criteria do not contain a specific criterion for
    a corridor recovering from a declared natural disaster or for post-disaster recovery. Hearing
    Tr. Vol. 4 at 55:4-23, PUC Interchange Item No. 6137.



                                              Page 3
 32. The April 12, 2022 tornado and the Cedar Valley community's ongoing recovery are
    relevant community-value, environmental-integrity, aesthetic-value, and prudent-routing
    considerations.
33. The record should not require a family and community already affected by tornado damage
    to absorb another permanent infrastructure burden where reasonable non-F20 alternatives
    exist.
34. Possible future development associated with Links F04, F20, F21, or any other link should
    not receive controlling route-selection weight unless supported by observable, measurable,
    and reliable record evidence.
35. Existing homes, existing agricultural operations, First Cedar Valley Baptist Church,
    existing community uses, tornado-recovery conditions, and Buttermilk Creek cultural-
    resource concerns are present and concrete factors that should receive greater weight than
    speculative future development.
36. Landowners on alternate or later-added routes did not receive the same meaningful
    opportunity as originally notified landowners to review environmental data, identify count
    errors, hire counsel, participate in route development, and advocate before Applicants
    changed or added links.
37. The unequal notice and participation opportunity is directly tied to record reliability
    because local landowners are often best able to identify missed habitable structures, local
    churches, cultural sites, drainage areas, storm-recovery issues, and conditions not visible
    from desktop data.
38. The Kevin Kennedy Initial Post-Hearing Brief supports giving weight to notice and
    community-values concerns where route links were added or revised after public meetings
    and affected landowners did not receive the same opportunity to participate. Kevin Kennedy
    Initial Post-Hearing Brief, PUC Interchange Item No. 6317.
39. OPUC recognized that pro se landowner concerns should receive equal footing and that
    notice asymmetry harmed landowners brought into the route after public meetings. OPUC
    Initial Post-Hearing Brief, PUC Interchange Item No. 6179.
40. Route 296 is a reasonable non-F20 route supported by Ms. Randolph and other parties.
41. Staff witness John Poole confirmed that Route 296 was his second-place route and ranked
    above Applicants' Route 894. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 91:21-92:4, PUC Interchange Item No.
    6137.
42. Route 899 removes Links F20 and F23 while remaining close to Route 894.
43. The Yates Keith Alliance, although supporting Route 894, stated it would not oppose Route
    899, a route very similar to 894 that accommodates the Howton opposition to F20/F23.
    Yates Keith Alliance Initial Post-Hearing Brief, PUC Interchange Item No. 6239.



                                             Page 4
 44. Route 499 removes the F20/F23 corridor while preserving the western alignment associated
    with Route 487.
45. Cross-examination showed that Route 499 has the same number of habitable structures as
    Route 487, the same length across endangered-species habitat, and a cost difference of
    approximately $2 million, or about one-tenth of one percent. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 205:11-
    207:10, PUC Interchange Item No. 6137.
46. At the link level, F21 is preferable to F20 because it avoids or reduces the concentrated
    residential, church, cultural-resource, tornado-recovery, and cumulative-infrastructure
    harms associated with F20.
47. The record contains feasible non-F20 alternatives that avoid the specific localized harms
    associated with Link F20 without defeating the project.
48. The record does not support certification of Route 894 or any route using Link F20.

                         II. PROPOSED CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
1.   The Public Utility Commission of Texas has jurisdiction over this proceeding under PURA
     Chapter 37, including PURA § 37.056.
2.   SOAH has jurisdiction over the hearing on the merits and preparation of a proposal for
     decision in this docket.
3.   Applicants bear the burden of proving that the route selected for certification meets the
     statutory and regulatory routing criteria.
4.   Under PURA § 37.056(c), the Commission must consider, among other applicable factors,
     community values, recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values,
     environmental integrity, and the probable improvement of service or lowering of cost to
     consumers.
5.   Under 16 Texas Administrative Code § 25.101(b)(3)(B), the Commission must consider,
     among other factors, community values, recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic
     values, environmental integrity, engineering constraints, costs, prudent avoidance, and use
     of existing compatible rights-of-way, property lines, and other natural or cultural features.
6.   Community values, historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, and prudent
     avoidance are broad enough to include a permanent encumbrance on an existing family
     homestead, agricultural operation, and future inheritance interest.
7.   Prudent avoidance requires meaningful consideration of habitable structures and human
     exposure and should not be satisfied by unverified desktop counts when local record
     evidence identifies a missed or disputed habitable structure.
8.   A route cannot be found to best meet the applicable routing criteria where a material link-
     level analysis is incomplete or unreliable on habitable structures, family-property impacts,


                                              Page 5
      community values, cultural resources, endangered-species concerns, historical and aesthetic
     values, environmental integrity, or archaeological sensitivity.
9.   Post-approval surveys, mitigation, and agency coordination may be appropriate compliance
     measures, but they do not substitute for an adequate comparative route-selection record.
10. The ALJs and Commission may recommend or approve a route other than Applicants'
    preferred or recommended route when the record supports a different route under the
    applicable statutory and regulatory criteria.
11. The ALJs and Commission may give reduced weight to route-selection justifications based
    on speculative future or potential development that is not supported by present, observable,
    and measurable record evidence.
12. The unequal and compressed notice period provided to later-added alternate-route
    landowners is relevant to the weight and reliability of the route-selection record, especially
    where those landowners identify material discrepancies after being brought into the case.
13. The record supports rejection of Route 894 and any route using Link F20.
14. The record supports selection of Route 296 as a reasonable non-F20 route.
15. In the alternative, if Route 296 is not selected, the record supports selection of Route 899,
    Route 499, Route 767, Route 295, or another route that avoids Link F20.

                        III. PROPOSED ORDERING PARAGRAPHS
       Ms. Randolph respectfully requests ordering paragraphs substantially similar to the
following:
1.   Applicants' Joint Application is granted only to the extent it authorizes amendment of the
     certificates of convenience and necessity for a route that avoids Link F20.
2.   Applicants' Route 894 is not approved.
3.   No route using Link F20 is approved.
4.   Route 296 is approved for the Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765-kV
     Transmission Line Project.
5.   In the alternative, if Route 296 is not approved, Applicants shall construct the project on
     Route 899, Route 499, Route 767, Route 295, or another route approved by the
     Commission that avoids Link F20.
6.   Applicants shall construct, operate, and maintain the transmission line in accordance with
     the Commission-approved route and the ordering paragraphs in the final order.
7.   Applicants shall use best management practices, prudent avoidance, and reasonable
     mitigation measures to minimize impacts to habitable structures, family residences,




                                              Page 6
      agricultural uses, community values, cultural resources, historical and aesthetic values,
     environmental integrity, and affected landowners.
8.   Before construction, Applicants shall conduct appropriate field verification for habitable
     structures, cultural resources, historical and archaeological resources, and endangered-
     species habitat along the approved route and shall not rely solely on desktop, aerial, or GIS
     review where field verification is necessary to protect affected landowners and resources.
9.   Applicants shall coordinate with appropriate federal, state, and local agencies, including the
     U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the Texas Historical Commission as applicable,
     regarding endangered-species habitat, cultural resources, historical resources, and
     archaeological sensitivity along the approved route.
10. Applicants shall obtain all permits, approvals, and authorizations required by law before
    beginning construction.
11. Applicants shall provide updated landowner notice and route information to affected
    landowners as required by Commission rules and the final order.
12. All other motions, requests for relief, or requested ordering paragraphs inconsistent with the
    final order are denied.

                                          IV. PRAYER
        For these reasons, Stacy Randolph respectfully requests that the Administrative Law
Judges adopt these Proposed Findings of Fact, Conclusions of Law, and Ordering Paragraphs;
recommend rejection of Applicants' Route 894 and any route using Link F20; recommend Route
296; or, in the alternative, recommend Route 899, Route 499, Route 767, Route 295, or another
route that avoids Link F20. Ms. Randolph further requests all other relief to which she may be
justly entitled.

Respectfully submitted,

/s/ Stacy Randolph
Stacy Randolph
Pro Se Intervenor
Daughter of Aaron Edward Howton and Nelda Howton
Future heir to the Howton properties
2519 Indian Mills Dr.
Salado, Texas 76571
Telephone: 512-966-5099
Email: randstay@gmail.com

                                CERTIFICATE OF SERVICE




                                              Page 7
         I certify that a copy of this document will be served on all parties of record in this
proceeding in accordance with SOAH Order No. 6 and the applicable orders and rules governing
service in this docket.
Date: June 26, 2026

/s/ Stacy Randolph
Stacy Randolph
Pro Se Intervenor




                                            Page 8

                                         1
 TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:
        Intervenor Stacy Randolph, appearing pro se, files this Reply to Initial Post-Hearing
Briefs as the daughter of Aaron Edward Howton and Nelda Howton and as an heir to the Howton
properties. Ms. Randolph respectfully replies to the briefs supporting Applicants' Route 894 or
any route using Link F20. She continues to oppose certification of any route using Link F20
because F20 would impose a permanent industrial burden on her parents' residence, agricultural
land, family inheritance interests, and the Cedar Valley community. The record supports
approval of a route that avoids Link F20, including Route 296, Route 899, Route 499, Route 767,
Route 295, or another non-F20 alternative.

                                   I. SUMMARY OF REPLY
         The briefs supporting Route 894 ask the Administrative Law Judges to rely heavily on
route-wide tables, generalized cost figures, reported habitable-structure counts, and assurances
that later mitigation will address site-specific concerns. That approach does not resolve the link-
level problems with F20. The record shows that the Applicants' environmental information was
developed primarily from desktop review, aerial review, GIS mapping, and other non-ground-
level sources. The cross-examination record then exposed discrepancies and omissions that
matter to route selection, including a disputed habitable-structure count, the treatment of First
Cedar Valley Baptist Church, the absence of F20-specific Golden-cheeked Warbler field
verification, and the failure to address Cedar Valley tornado recovery.
        Ms. Randolph's position is different from a landowner who is only concerned about a
current construction inconvenience. She is Aaron Edward Howton and Nelda Howton's daughter
and an heir to their properties. The route decision will determine whether the next generation
inherits a family homestead and working rural property or a property permanently burdened by a
765-kV transmission line. Community values, historical and aesthetic values, environmental
integrity, and prudent avoidance should be applied with that long-term family impact in mind.
        Applicants should not be allowed to rely on possible future developments when it helps
justify or distinguish particular links, including Links F04, F20, and F21, unless those
developments are supported by observable and measurable evidence in the record. The
Commission's routing decision should rest on present, reliable, and verifiable facts. Speculative
future development should not outweigh existing homes, an existing church, established
agricultural uses, actual tornado damage, known cultural-resource concerns, and local evidence
that was not adequately captured by desktop data.
        The record also raises a fairness and notice problem. Landowners on alternate or later-
added routes were not given the same meaningful opportunity as the originally notified
landowners to review the environmental data, identify count errors, hire counsel, participate in
route development, and advocate for route changes before the Applicants changed or added
links. That unequal process matters because the errors now identified on F20 are exactly the
kinds of errors that timely landowner participation can reveal.
      The narrowest and fairest remedy is to reject Link F20. Route 296 remains Ms.
Randolph's preferred non-F20 route. If the ALJs are not persuaded that Route 296 should be


                                                 2
 selected, Route 899, Route 499, Route 767, Route 295, or another non-F20 route would still
avoid the concentrated harms to the Howton family property, First Cedar Valley Baptist Church,
Golden-cheeked Warbler habitat concerns, Buttermilk Creek cultural-resource concerns, and the
tornado-damaged Cedar Valley community.

      II. STACY RANDOLPH HAS A DISTINCT FAMILY AND HEIR INTEREST
        Ms. Randolph has a direct family interest in this routing decision. She is the daughter of
Aaron Edward Howton and Nelda Howton, and she is an heir to the Howton properties. Her
concern is not limited to a temporary construction period. The 765-kV line would be a long-term
burden on the property that she and future family members expect to inherit, use, maintain, and
protect.
        The Howton property is not vacant land waiting for a utility corridor. It is a family
residence and working rural property used for cattle, horses, poultry, gardening, hunting, outdoor
family activities, and ordinary agricultural operations. Stacy Randolph's Initial Brief describes
the Howton property as a homesite and rural property with livestock, family uses, and future
inheritance interests. Stacy Randolph Initial Post-Hearing Brief, PUC Interchange Item No.
6210.
        The ALJs should therefore evaluate Link F20 not only as a line on a routing table, but as
a permanent encumbrance on an existing family homestead, agricultural operation, and future
inheritance. The Commission's routing factors are broad enough to account for those facts under
community values, historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, and prudent
avoidance.

   III. APPLICANTS' DESKTOP AND AERIAL DATA WERE NOT ADEQUATELY
                        VERIFIED ON THE GROUND
        The record establishes that the Applicants relied on desktop data, aerial review, GIS
mapping, and later promised mitigation rather than boots-on-the-ground verification before
relying on Link F20. That matters because the purpose of this hearing is to compare routes now,
based on a reliable record, not to defer essential verification until after a route is approved.
       Cross-examination confirmed that Applicants' witness did not personally walk Link F20
and did not obtain the kind of local field information necessary to identify site-specific
constraints before relying on F20 in Route 894. Hearing Tr. Vol. 2 at 120:18-124:8, PUC
Interchange Item No. 6137.
        The consequences of that lack of field verification were shown in the record. The Carl
Simpson residence was identified as approximately 383 feet from Link F20, within the 500-foot
habitable-structure distance, and Mr. Marusak acknowledged that, based on the graphic, it
appeared to be within that distance. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 51:8-52:21, PUC Interchange Item No.
6137. Mr. Marusak further acknowledged that, if the structure meets Applicants' habitable-
structure standard, Applicants would adjust the F20 count. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 52:15-21, PUC
Interchange Item No. 6137.



                                                3
         The same problem appears in the environmental record. Mr. Marusak confirmed that no
site-specific Golden-cheeked Warbler habitat field survey was conducted on Link F20 before
route selection and that the F20 endangered-species figure was based on GIS/USFWS mapping
rather than field verification. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 52:23-54:8, PUC Interchange Item No. 6137.
Applicants should not receive route-selection credit for unverified desktop numbers when local
evidence and cross-examination show the numbers may be incomplete.
        For Ms. Randolph, this is not a technical complaint. The desktop-versus-field problem
affects the inheritance, use, and value of her family property. A missed home, an omitted church,
unverified endangered-species habitat, and overlooked tornado recovery can change how the
statutory routing factors should be balanced.

 IV. SPECULATIVE FUTURE DEVELOPMENT SHOULD NOT CONTROL LINK OR
                         ROUTE SELECTION
        Applicants and some route supporters have used possible future development as part of
their route and link arguments. Ms. Randolph respectfully submits that possible future
development should not be used selectively to justify or disfavor links such as F04, F20, or F21
unless the development is supported by observable, measurable, and reliable record evidence.
        The ALJs should apply Commission precedent and evidentiary fairness consistently: a
future development that is not presently observable or supported by measurable facts should not
be given controlling weight over existing residences, existing agricultural operations, an existing
church, existing community uses, and verified local conditions. Otherwise, speculative
development becomes a tool for shifting impacts away from one group of landowners and onto
another.
        This point is especially important to Ms. Randolph because the Howton property is an
existing family residence and agricultural property, not a hypothetical future use. First Cedar
Valley Baptist Church is an existing community resource. The Cedar Valley tornado damage is
an existing community burden. Buttermilk Creek and the surrounding cultural-resource concerns
are existing site-specific concerns. Those real and present factors should receive more weight
than speculative development claims.

   V. ALTERNATE-ROUTE LANDOWNERS DID NOT RECEIVE THE SAME FAIR
              NOTICE AND PARTICIPATION OPPORTUNITY
        The record also supports giving reduced weight to route changes that resulted from an
unequal notice process. Original-notice landowners had a longer opportunity to review the route
data, retain counsel, identify mistakes, and advocate for changes. Landowners affected by
alternate or later-added routes did not receive the same meaningful opportunity before the
Applicants changed or added links.
       This unfairness is directly tied to the reliability of the record. Local landowners are often
the people most able to identify a missed habitable structure, a local church or cultural site, a
drainage area, a storm-recovery issue, or a condition not visible from desktop data. When



                                                  4
 alternate-route landowners are brought into the process late, the Applicants' data errors are less
likely to be corrected before route recommendations harden.
        The Kevin Kennedy Initial Post-Hearing Brief supports giving weight to notice and
community-values concerns where route links were added or revised after public meetings and
affected landowners did not receive the same opportunity to participate. Kevin Kennedy Initial
Post-Hearing Brief, PUC Interchange Item No. 6317. OPUC likewise recognized that pro se
landowner concerns should receive equal footing and that notice asymmetry harmed landowners
brought into the route after public meetings. OPUC Initial Post-Hearing Brief, PUC Interchange
Item No. 6179.
         Ms. Randolph asks the ALJs to account for that process unfairness when weighing Route
894 and Link F20. The record should not reward a route-selection process in which early-noticed
landowners had time and resources to influence route changes while later-affected families were
left to identify errors under compressed deadlines.

VI. LINK F20 UNDERVALUES COMMUNITY VALUES, CHURCH, CULTURAL, AND
                     ENVIRONMENTAL CONCERNS
A. First Cedar Valley Baptist Church
        First Cedar Valley Baptist Church is not merely a structure near a line on a map. The
record identifies the church as a longstanding community, cultural, historical, and aesthetic
resource near Link F20. Aaron Edward Howton's filings identify the church as established in or
about 1942 and located approximately 690 to 720 feet from the F20 centerline. Aaron Edward
Howton Initial Post-Hearing Brief, PUC Interchange Item No. 6257; filing regarding First Cedar
Valley Baptist Church, PUC Interchange Item No. 5925.
        Stacy Randolph's own Initial Brief emphasized the church's role as a community and
disaster gathering place. Stacy Randolph Initial Post-Hearing Brief, PUC Interchange Item No.
6210. A routing analysis that shows zero cultural resources for F20 is materially incomplete
when a longstanding church and community landmark lies within the review area.
B. Golden-cheeked Warbler habitat and USFWS concerns
       The environmental record for F20 is incomplete for the same reason: Applicants relied on
mapping and promised later coordination rather than field verification before route selection. The
record cited by Aaron Edward Howton and Jason Aaron Howton explains that Applicants did not
conduct F20-specific Golden-cheeked Warbler field verification and did not provide comparable
F20-specific U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service validation before relying on the F20 environmental
data. Aaron Edward Howton Initial Post-Hearing Brief, PUC Interchange Item No. 6257; Jason
Aaron Howton Initial Brief, PUC Interchange Item No. 6250.
        Post-approval coordination does not cure a route-selection defect. The ALJs must
compare F20 against alternatives before approval. If F20's endangered-species number was an
unverified desktop conclusion, it should not be treated as a reliable advantage over non-F20
routes.



                                                 5
 C. Buttermilk Creek, historical, archaeological, and cultural-resource concerns
        Buttermilk Creek and the surrounding area raise serious historical, archaeological, and
cultural-resource concerns. Aaron Edward Howton's Initial Post-Hearing Brief argues that
Applicants did not field-survey the archaeologically sensitive Buttermilk Creek drainage before
selecting F20 and that Table 7-3 shows F20 crosses high archaeological-potential areas. Aaron
Edward Howton Initial Post-Hearing Brief, PUC Interchange Item No. 6257.
       The Route 894 briefs ask the ALJs to rely on desktop cultural-resource tables. Ms.
Randolph asks the ALJs to give greater weight to local record evidence showing an omitted
church, an unsurveyed sensitive drainage area, and cultural-resource concerns that should not be
dismissed by a generalized table.

VII. TORNADO RECOVERY AND CUMULATIVE BURDEN WEIGH AGAINST LINK
                              F20
       The April 12, 2022 EF-3 tornado through Cedar Valley is relevant to community values,
environmental integrity, aesthetic values, and prudent routing. The tornado did not merely create
temporary damage; it left a rural community still recovering. Ms. Randolph's family property and
surrounding area should not be forced to absorb another permanent infrastructure burden when
reasonable non-F20 alternatives exist.
        Cross-examination confirmed that the Environmental Assessment did not reference the
April 12, 2022 EF-3 tornado through Cedar Valley. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 54:10-14, PUC
Interchange Item No. 6137. The witness also confirmed that the routing criteria do not contain a
specific criterion for a corridor recovering from a declared natural disaster or post-disaster
recovery. Hearing Tr. Vol. 4 at 55:4-23, PUC Interchange Item No. 6137.
       That omission matters. A table that does not measure disaster recovery cannot fairly

                          II. PROPOSED CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
1.    The Public Utility Commission of Texas has jurisdiction over this proceeding under PURA
      Chapter 37, including PURA § 37.056.

2.    SOAH has jurisdiction over the hearing on the merits and preparation of a proposal for
      decision in this docket.
3.    Applicants bear the burden of proving that the route selected for certification meets the
      statutory and regulatory routing criteria.
4.    Under PURA § 37.056(c), the Commission must consider, among other applicable factors,
      community values, recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values,
      environmental integrity, and the probable improvement of service or lowering of cost to
      consumers.
5.    Under 16 Texas Administrative Code § 25.101(b)(3)(B), the Commission must consider,
      among other factors, community values, recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic
      values, environmental integrity, engineering constraints, costs, prudent avoidance, and use
      of existing compatible rights-of-way, property lines, and other natural or cultural features.
6.    Community values, historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, and prudent
      avoidance are broad enough to include a permanent encumbrance on an existing family
      homestead, agricultural operation, and future inheritance interest.
7.    Prudent avoidance requires meaningful consideration of habitable structures and human
      exposure and should not be satisfied by unverified desktop counts when local record
      evidence identifies a missed or disputed habitable structure.
8.    A route cannot be found to best meet the applicable routing criteria where a material link-
      level analysis is incomplete or unreliable on habitable structures, family-property impacts,



                                               Page 5
       community values, cultural resources, endangered-species concerns, historical and aesthetic
      values, environmental integrity, or archaeological sensitivity.
9.    Post-approval surveys, mitigation, and agency coordination may be appropriate compliance
      measures, but they do not substitute for an adequate comparative route-selection record.
10.   The ALJs and Commission may recommend or approve a route other than Applicants'
      preferred or recommended route when the record supports a different route under the
      applicable statutory and regulatory criteria.
11.   The ALJs and Commission may give reduced weight to route-selection justifications based
      on speculative future or potential development that is not supported by present, observable,
      and measurable record evidence.
12.   The unequal and compressed notice period provided to later-added alternate-route
      landowners is relevant to the weight and reliability of the route-selection record, especially
      where those landowners identify material discrepancies after being brought into the case.
13.   The record supports rejection of Route 894 and any route using Link F20.

14.   The record supports selection of Route 296 as a reasonable non-F20 route.

15.   In the alternative, if Route 296 is not selected, the record supports selection of Route 899,
      Route 499, Route 767, Route 295, or another route that avoids Link F20.
